Behavioral Activation.title: Depression in autism spectrum disorder: a scoping review of pharmacologic, neuromodulation, and psychosocial interventions.
Behavioral Activation.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Major depressive disorder is common in autism spectrum disorder, but diagnosis and treatment are complicated by symptom overlap, atypical presentations, alexithymia, and limited ASD-specific evidence.
METHODS: We conducted a scoping review of PubMed, PsycINFO, and reference lists for studies published from 1995 through 2025 examining pharmacologic, neuromodulation, and psychosocial interventions for depressive symptoms in ASD.
RESULTS: Psychosocial interventions, including autism-adapted cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based therapy, dialectical behavior therapy-informed approaches, behavioral activation, PEERS, exercise, and animal-assisted therapy, were associated with improvements in depressive symptoms in open-label studies and small randomized trials. Neuromodulation findings were preliminary, while evidence for electroconvulsive therapy and deep brain stimulation was primarily case-based. Pharmacologic recommendations were based largely on expert consensus and indirect evidence rather than ASD-specific controlled trials.
DISCUSSION: Depression treatment in ASD remains understudied. Larger controlled trials using ASD-validated depression measures, broader representation across support needs, and assessment of functional and long-term outcomes are needed.

Behavioral Activation.title: Incorporating Objective Behavioral and Biological Measures in a Large-Scale Decentralized Mobile Health Trial for Depression: Randomized Controlled Trial.
Behavioral Activation.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Decentralized (ie, fully remote) clinical trials (DCTs) offer a scalable and ecologically valid approach to evaluating digital mental health interventions (DMHIs). Yet, incorporating objective measures of well-being within DCTs poses novel methodological and feasibility challenges that can limit the rigor and precision of data collection in the field.
OBJECTIVE: We recently conducted the Behavior, Biology, and Well-being (BeWell) Study, a large-scale, 3-arm randomized DCT evaluating the Healthy Minds Program app (Humin)-a self-guided DMHI that includes didactic well-being information and meditation components. The current paper's objective is to describe the methodological approach to collecting and processing a multimodal battery of psychological (questionnaires and structured clinical interview), biological (blood and stool assays), and behavioral (stimulus-elicited affect [SEA] task, video log, and Mnemonic Similarity Task [MST]) measures, longitudinally across baseline, the 4-week intervention period, and 17-week follow-up. Secondarily, we evaluate its feasibility.
METHODS: The BeWell Study methodology is described. Descriptive statistics characterized recruitment and retention, as well as data completion and data quality. Binary logistic regressions evaluated whether recruitment sources, demographics, and depression severity predicted measure completion and data quality.
RESULTS: From June 1, 2022, through July 15, 2024, 52,052 individuals started the screening questionnaire. Of these, 2.22% (n=1156 participants; mean age 38.69, SD 12.14 years; women=75.50%; non-Hispanic White=68.88%) completed the screener, met eligibility criteria (including elevated depressive symptoms [Patient Health Questionnaire-9 [PHQ-9] score≥5]), completed baseline measures, were enrolled, and were randomized. Participants were recruited from Craigslist (694/1154, 60.14%), a US-based advertisement website, and university email messages (107/1154, 9.27%); participants were enrolled from every US state. Across the study, 84% (971/1156) of participants were retained (completed ≥1 measure at 17-week follow-up). Across time points, ≥81.40% (941/1156) of participants completed questionnaires and ≥75.17% (869/1156) completed biological samples. Of those completing questionnaires, ≥84.14% (796/946) completed SEA and video log tasks and ≥91.75% (868/946) completed the MST. Of completed assessments, high-quality or analyzable data rates across all time points were ≥97.89% (926/946) for questionnaires, ≥90.20% (773/857) for SEA, ≥84.60% (725/857) for video logs, ≥94.20% (1056/1121) for the MST, ≥98.84% (849/859) for dried blood spots, and ≥99.43% (865/870) for microbiome samples. Greater depressive symptoms at screening, but not age, predicted completion of baseline measures (odds ratios 0.96-0.99; P<.001). For enrolled participants, recruitment sources and baseline depressive symptoms were not predictive of data completion or quality. Older age and having a college degree predicted significantly higher rates of data completion across all data types (questionnaire, behavioral, and biological) at week 4 or week 17 follow-ups.
CONCLUSIONS: This methodological approach offers one model of incorporating objective measures of well-being into DCTs testing DMHIs. Implications and limitations of our approach are discussed.

Behavioral Activation.title: Right putaminal gray matter change tracks psychomotor recovery after accelerated iTBS in melancholic treatment-resistant depression.
Behavioral Activation.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychomotor retardation is a prominent and disabling feature of melancholic depression. Accelerated intermittent theta-burst stimulation (aiTBS) may hasten antidepressant effects, but neural substrates of early symptom improvement remain unclear. Given the central role of frontostriatal circuitry in motivation and behavioral activation, structural alterations in the striatum may represent a possible neural substrate of early therapeutic change.
METHODS: Structural MRI was acquired from 61 patients with melancholic TRD and 77 healthy controls, and voxel-based morphometry was used to assess baseline striatal gray matter volume differences. Patients then underwent a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial of left dorsolateral prefrontal aiTBS, comprising 20 sessions over four days. In 50 patients with complete pre- and post-treatment data, we tested whether GMV change in the baseline-identified striatal region was associated with clinical change in the active and sham groups (n = 25 each).
RESULTS: Patients showed greater right putamen GMV than controls at baseline. After active aiTBS, greater right putamen GMV increase was associated with greater psychomotor retardation improvement. This association was absent after sham stimulation and was not observed for overall depression severity.
CONCLUSION: The right putamen appears structurally altered in melancholic TRD. After active aiTBS, short-term putamen GMV increase was associated with psychomotor rather than broader depressive improvement. This pattern should not be interpreted as structural normalization but may reflect a relationship between putaminal change and early psychomotor recovery.

Behavioral Activation.title: Outcomes of Mindful Mood Balance for Moms, online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for perinatal depressive relapse prevention in the USA: a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic randomised clinical trial.
Behavioral Activation.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Effective and accessible approaches to prevent depressive relapse and reduce symptoms are crucial for addressing the major public health problem of depression among perinatal women. We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of Mindful Mood Balance (MMB) for Moms plus usual care (hereafter MMB for Moms)-a web-based mindfulness-based cognitive therapy programme customised for perinatal women-compared with usual care only, in reducing depressive relapse and symptoms.
METHODS: This single-blind, randomised clinical trial was done across the USA, in euthymic pregnant women with recurrent depression who were on recent or current antidepressant medication. Recruitment occurred from March 7, 2019, to July 8, 2020 (data collection was completed Sept 12, 2021). Participants were randomly assigned to MMB for Moms, or usual care. Primary outcomes were reduction in depressive relapse risk and symptom burden, assessed using the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview and Patient Health Questionaire-9, respectively, across the study period. Outcomes were assessed from baseline until 6-months postpartum in three phases (intervention, end of intervention to delivery, and postpartum). The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03623620, and is complete.
FINDINGS: Participants were recruited between March 7, 2019, and July 8, 2020. Data from 500 randomly assigned participants (mean age 32 years [SD 4·5] and mean 11·5 [2·8] weeks gestation), were analysed as the intention-to-treat sample. Of the 500 participants (249 assigned to MMB for Moms and 251 assigned to usual care), 383 [77%] provided assessment data at 3 months and 389 [78%] at 6 months postpartum. MMB for Moms had significantly lower risk of depressive relapse compared with usual care during the full trial period (up to 6 months postpartum): 81 (33%) of 249 participants assigned to MMB for Moms and 111 (44%) of 251 participants in usual care had depressive relapse (hazard ratio 0·74 [95% CI 0·56-0·99]; p=0·045; adjusted false discovery rate p=0·045). MMB for Moms was also associated with a significant reduction in depression symptom burden during the 12 week intervention phase (average decrease of 0·75 [SE 0·13] in the MMB for Moms group and 0·31 [0·13] in the usual care group) but not during the full trial period (average decrease of 0·61 [SE 0·18] in the MMB for Moms group and 0·54 [0·17] in the usual care group).
INTERPRETATION: MMB for Moms resulted in lower risk of relapse compared with usual care, and lower depression symptom burden during the intervention phase, potentially offering an effective non-pharmacological support option for depression relapse prevention during the perinatal period with positive implications for public health practice.
FUNDING: US National Institutes of Health and US National Institute of Mental Health.

Behavioral Activation.title: Behavioral Activation for Depression and Glycemic Control in Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Behavioral Activation.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Depression in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) hinders self-management and glycemic control. Behavioral activation (BA), by increasing participation in positive activities, holds promise for simultaneously improving depressive symptoms and diabetes outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated the effects of BA or BA-based interventions on depressive symptoms, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), diabetes self-efficacy, and self-management behaviors in adults with T2DM, and summarized their implementation characteristics.
METHODOLOGY: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, PsycINFO, CNKI, VIP, and Wanfang Data were searched from inception to February 1, 2026. Interventional studies assessing BA or BA-based interventions in adults with T2DM and reporting at least one prespecified outcome were included. Quantitative meta-analyses were restricted to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and conducted using random-effects models. Implementation characteristics from all included studies were narratively synthesized.
RESULTS: Six studies involving 252 participants met the inclusion criteria, including five RCTs and one single-arm pre-post study. The meta-analysis suggested a reduction in depressive symptoms (SMD = -0.81, 95% CI: -1.22 to -0.41, p < 0.001), but no statistically significant effects on HbA1c (MD = -0.04%, 95% CI: -0.30 to 0.22, p = 0.76), diabetes self-efficacy (SMD = 0.03, 95% CI: -0.30 to 0.35, p = 0.87), or self-management behaviors (SMD = 0.04, 95% CI: -0.23 to 0.32, p = 0.77). Narrative synthesis indicated that BA interventions varied in delivery format, dosage, provider background, and integration with diabetes-specific content. Most interventions were delivered by non-mental health professionals and incorporated core BA components such as activity monitoring and goal setting.
CONCLUSION: BA may reduce depressive symptoms in adults with T2DM, whereas its effects on glycemic control, diabetes self-efficacy, and self-management behaviors remain uncertain. BA has been delivered in flexible formats and may have potential for integration into diabetes care, but larger, well-powered RCTs with longer follow-up are needed to determine whether diabetes-specific BA can improve behavioral and physiological outcomes.

Circadian Synchronization.title: The impact of bright light therapy on non-motor symptoms in patients with Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
Circadian Synchronization.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The non-motor symptoms of Parkinson's patients seriously affect their quality of life. This meta-analysis intended to systematically examine the beneficial effect of bright light therapy (BLT) on non-motor symptoms in individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD).
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase, Ovid Medline, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), WanFang VIP and CBM to comprehensively collect RCTS and NRCTS relevant to BLT for Parkinson's disease. Data extraction and literature screening were carried out separately by two researchers, and used the RoB2 tool and ROBINS-I tool to evaluate the risk of bias for the two types of studies, respectively. Software such as RevMan5.4 and Stata 18.0 were used to analyze the data.
RESULTS: Compared with dim light, BLT has a considerable benefit in improving the nighttime sleep of people with Parkinson's disease. However, its therapeutic effects on depression, anxiety, exhaustion, cognition, sleep quality and quality of life are not superior to those of dim light. Moreover, the distance of the light source will alter the therapeutic effect of BLT on nighttime sleep and daytime sleepiness.
RESULTS: Compared with dim light, BLT has a considerable benefit in improving the nighttime sleep of people with PD. However, its therapeutic effects on depression, anxiety, fatigue, cognition, sleep quality and quality of life are not superior to those of dim light. Moreover, the distance of the light source will alter the therapeutic effect of BLT on nighttime sleep and daytime sleepiness.
CONCLUSION: BLT can be used to treat the non-motor symptoms of PD and may become a practical option for home self-management. However, the ideal therapy parameters (such as intensity, distance, cycle, etc.) still need further research.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251047102, identifier (CRD420251047102).

Circadian Synchronization.title: The impact of timing on bright light therapy: Alleviating anhedonia and circadian rhythm disturbances in depression patients: a randomized controlled trial.
Circadian Synchronization.abstract: This study aimed to determine the effectiveness of different times of bright light therapy (BLT) in alleviating anhedonia and circadian rhythm disturbances in depression patients. The study also explored whether the positive effects of BLT on anhedonia in depression were associated with changes in melatonin and cortisol indices throughout the treatment period. In this single-blind, placebo-controlled study, 81 patients were randomly assigned to one of four groups: morning BLT group, morning placebo group, evening BLT group, or evening placebo group. Participants in the BLT groups received BLT at 10,000 lx, while those in the placebo groups were exposed at 100 lx for 30 min daily over two weeks. The primary outcome measure was the Revised Physical Anhedonia Scale (RPAS) score. Secondary outcome measures included salivary melatonin and cortisol levels, as well as the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) score. The morning BLT group showed a significant delay in the melatonin peak phase and an improvement in RPAS scores compared to the morning placebo group. A correlation between changes in RPAS scores and melatonin peak phase was observed (P = 0.048) after morning BLT, with multiple linear regression analysis further confirming this relationship (P = 0.026). These findings suggest that morning BLT significantly alleviates anhedonia in depression, an effect associated with delayed melatonin peak phase. Depressive symptoms improved following both morning and evening BLT. These results highlight the potential of bright light therapy as a non-pharmacological treatment option, with morning administration showing particular benefit for anhedonia.

Circadian Synchronization.title: The effect of bright light therapy on glycemic control and cortisol rhythmicity in depression: a randomized controlled trial.
Circadian Synchronization.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Depressed patients with comorbid metabolic disorders have poorer quality of life and prognosis. Pharmacological interventions carries risks of liver and kidney toxicity, which highlights the need for safer non-pharmacological alternatives. Experimental data suggest that light exposure modulates cortisol secretion, thereby influencing metabolic outcomes in depression. We hypothesized that bright light therapy may ameliorate metabolic disturbances by modulating cortisol secretion.
METHODS: In this randomized controlled trial, hospitalized patients with depression were assigned to receive either bright light therapy (BLT) or dim-light control condition. The pre-specified primary endpoint was the change in fasting blood glucose (FBG) and cortisol rhythm indices from baseline to post-treatment. Secondary endpoints included changes in other glycolipid parameters, and scores on the Hamilton Depression (HAMD) and Anxiety (HAMA) scales. Treatment effects were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models with baseline adjustment.
RESULTS: After the 2-week intervention, the BLT group showed a significant reduction in fasting blood glucose (95% CI: 0.280 to 0.600; p < 0.001) and cortisol mesor (95% CI: -2.677 to -0.064; p = 0.040) compared to the control group. Within the BLT group, the change in FBG was positively associated with the change in cortisol mesor after adjusting for covariates (β = 0.053, 95% CI: 0.016 to 0.122, p = 0.036).
CONCLUSIONS: The findings of this study support a potential mechanism whereby BLT modulates cortisol rhythmicity, which in turn may contribute to improved glycemic control, pointing to its potential therapeutic benefit for addressing metabolic disturbances in depression.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://www.chictr.org.cn/bin/project/edit?pid=260569, identifier ChiCTR2500097364.

Circadian Synchronization.title: Bright light therapy influences glymphatic system function in individuals with subthreshold depression: a randomized clinical trial.
Circadian Synchronization.abstract: Glymphatic system dysfunction is a potential early biomarker for neuropsychiatric disorders. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of bright light therapy (BLT) on the glymphatic system in individuals with subthreshold depression (StD) and its connections to brain activity, inflammatory cytokines, and depressive symptoms. A randomized placebo-controlled trial assigned adults with StD (N = 110) to 8 weeks of morning BLT (5000 lx, 30 min/day; n = 57) or placebo (inactive device; n = 53). Depression severity (primary outcome, including anhedonia), glymphatic markers (diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space [DTI-ALPS] index, free water [FW], perivascular space volume), regional homogeneity (ReHo; functional MRI), and serum pro-inflammatory cytokines were assessed at baseline and post-treatment. Compared to placebo, BLT significantly relieved depressive symptoms, increased DTI-ALPS index, and decreased FW from baseline to post-treatment. BLT also increased ReHo in the left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and decreased levels of interleukin-9 and tumor necrosis factor-β. Changes in the DTI-ALPS index correlated with ameliorated depressive symptoms, increased ReHo in the SFG, and decreased inflammatory cytokine levels. Additionally, the pairwise interaction effects between glymphatic markers, ReHo values, and serum levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines were independent predictors of improvements in depressive symptoms, particularly anhedonia. BLT may influence glymphatic function in StD, with enhanced glymphatic function correlated with reduced inflammation, enhanced prefrontal cortex activity, and symptom amelioration.

Circadian Synchronization.title: Efficacy of a portable BLT device on sleep and depressive symptoms in major depressive disorder: A double-blind randomized study.
Circadian Synchronization.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability worldwide and is often associated with anxiety and sleep disturbances. About one-third of patients do not achieve adequate response to pharmacological treatments, underscoring the need for adjunctive non-pharmacological therapies. Bright light therapy (BLT) has shown efficacy in MDD, but conventional devices require patients to remain stationary, limiting adherence. Portable BLT devices may improve convenience and daily integration. This study assessed the efficacy of a portable BLT device on mood, anxiety, and sleep over 8 weeks.
METHODS: LUMIDEP was a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Adults with MDD were randomized to receive active portable BLT or a visually identical placebo. Final analyses included 18 patients (BLT n = 6; placebo n = 12). Patients underwent 30-min daily sessions for 8 weeks while continuing pharmacological treatments. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), anxiety with the Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAM-A), and sleep with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS).
RESULTS: Baseline PSQI scores were higher in the BLT group. After 8 weeks, PSQI scores improved within the BLT group, while remaining stable in the placebo group, resulting in no significant between-group difference. No significant differences were observed between groups in HAM-A or MADRS.
CONCLUSIONS: Portable BLT appeared to improve sleep quality but did not significantly reduce depressive or anxiety symptoms. Interpretation is limited by group differences, treatment heterogeneity, and small sample size. Larger, stratified trials are warranted to clarify the efficacy of portable BLT in MDD.

Streak break shame vs Resilience.title: Internet-delivered self-help acceptance and commitment therapy for family carers of people with dementia (iACT4CARERS): a mixed-methods process evaluation of reach and recruitment.
Streak break shame vs Resilience.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: A mixed-methods process evaluation was conducted alongside a randomised controlled trial of iACT4CARERS, an eight-session, online, self-help Acceptance and Commitment Therapy intervention with minimal therapist support for family carers of people with dementia. The study examined the reach of the intervention and factors influencing recruitment to inform equitable implementation.
METHODS: Demographic data from 565 screened carers and interviews with 30 referrers across UK health services were analysed.
RESULTS: The screened sample was predominantly aged 50-79 years (82.5%), female (77%), and White (91.7%). Five themes were identified: referrers' coordinated referrals, mutual motivation, and community outreach supported engagement; referrers' trust-building, tailored communication, and timely approaches facilitated participation; carers' time constraints and referrers' assumptions about older carers' digital skills influenced recruitment; proactive outreach was important for engaging ethnic minority carers; and cultural perceptions of mental health created barriers to participation.
CONCLUSIONS: The sample was broadly comparable with previous estimates of the UK dementia carer population. For the equitable implementation of interventions such as iACT4CARERS, coordinated recruitment across health, social care, and voluntary organisations, alongside centralised intervention delivery, may be critical. Outreach can be further strengthened by enhancing referrers' communication and empowerment skills, including challenging assumptions about older carers' digital abilities.

Streak break shame vs Resilience.title: Effects of acceptance and commitment therapy on psychological and health-related outcomes in stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Streak break shame vs Resilience.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide and is frequently accompanied by psychological and functional impairments. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a third-wave behavioral intervention focusing on psychological flexibility, has been increasingly applied in stroke rehabilitation. Although previous reviews have suggested beneficial effects of ACT in stroke patients, whether these benefits persist in the short term after the intervention ends, and the certainty of the evidence, remain unclear.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261325108). Randomized controlled trials evaluating ACT in stroke patients were included. Pooled effects were calculated using random-effects models, with separate analyses for post-intervention and follow-up outcomes. Sources of heterogeneity were explored using subgroup analyses and meta-regression. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework.
RESULTS: Twenty-two RCTs involving 1,975 participants were included. ACT may be associated with reductions in depressive symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = -1.32, 95% CI: -1.80 to -0.84; follow-up: SMD = -0.76, 95% CI: -1.07 to -0.45) and anxiety symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = -1.36, 95% CI: -1.90 to -0.82; follow-up: SMD = -0.51, 95% CI: -1.42 to 0.40, not significant); depressive symptoms remained statistically significant at follow-up. Heterogeneity was considerable for both outcomes at post-intervention (I2 = 93.68% for depression and 93.60% for anxiety), so the pooled estimates represent average effects across studies. ACT may also be associated with improvements in psychological flexibility, quality of life, and sleep quality; however, these outcomes were based on a limited number of studies and showed considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 74.68 to 92.26%), so they should be interpreted cautiously. However, no statistically significant effects were observed for activities of daily living, neurological function, or hope. ACT did not appear to increase dropout rates in the available studies (K = 16; RR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.58-1.69). Meta-regression analyses indicated that intervention duration may not be a significant moderator of treatment effects. The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, mainly due to risk of bias and inconsistency.
CONCLUSION: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy may be a useful adjunctive intervention for improving psychological outcomes in people with stroke. However, evidence for functional recovery remains insufficient. Future high-quality RCTs with standardized protocols, larger samples, and longer follow-up are needed to confirm the long-term effectiveness of ACT.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifer CRD420261325108.

Streak break shame vs Resilience.title: Self-disgust and the body as a target in self-harm and suicidal behavior: A narrative review.
Streak break shame vs Resilience.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
Streak break shame vs Resilience.abstract: Self-harm and suicidal behavior are commonly framed as failures of emotion regulation, yet the emotions that make the body the target of harm remain under-specified. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on self-disgust as a candidate mechanism in non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) and in suicidal ideation and behavior. Self-disgust is an aversive self-directed emotion organized around the appraisal of the self, and often the body, as revolting or contaminated. Cross-sectional studies consistently link self-disgust with NSSI, suicidal ideation, and suicide-risk scores, and qualitative accounts place it at the center of some suicidal crises. Longitudinal studies from China suggest it mediates reciprocal links between emotional abuse and suicidal ideation and a path from body-image concerns to NSSI. Two prospective studies testing different roles did not support them, and the only induction study of self-harm urges is equivocal. In some studies, self-disgust explains variance beyond depression and constructs of the interpersonal theory of suicide. Its boundaries with shame and self-criticism are contested, and, across disorders, associations shrink when other negative self-referential emotions are controlled for. The central proposal, that the contamination-and-elimination logic of disgust explains why distress is enacted on the body, builds on earlier suggestions and remains an untested hypothesis. On this hypothesis, self-disgust is an embodied emotion whose action tendency of cleansing and removal may correspond to the phenomenology of cutting and, in some people, to a wish to eliminate a self experienced as contaminated. Implications for assessment and intervention, which remain untested, are outlined with falsifiable predictions for research.

Streak break shame vs Resilience.title: A pilot feasibility randomised controlled trial of an online cancer bereavement group.
Streak break shame vs Resilience.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bereavement following the death of a loved one from cancer presents unique challenges related to anticipatory stressors, caregiving demands, and the illness trajectory. Although online bereavement interventions may improve access to support, evidence for therapist-led online groups remains limited. This pilot randomised controlled trial evaluated the feasibility, acceptability and preliminary effectiveness of an online therapeutic group intervention for adults bereaved by cancer.
METHODS: In this longitudinal pilot RCT, adults bereaved by cancer were randomised to receive the intervention immediately or following a three-month wait-list period. The intervention comprised eight online group sessions delivered over 12 weeks, integrating trauma-informed cognitive behavioural therapy, compassion-focused therapy and psychoeducation. Primary outcomes were feasibility and acceptability. Secondary outcomes included prolonged grief, depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, self-compassion, and social disconnection, assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and three-month follow-up.
RESULTS: Of 124 randomised participants, 100 (80.6%) commenced the allocated intervention and 97 contributed sufficient data for primary analyses. The study met pre-specified feasibility and acceptability criteria, although patterns of attrition differed according to trial stage. Non-commencement following allocation was higher in the immediate intervention groups (27.0 vs 11.5%) whereas withdrawal after intervention commencement was higher in the waitlist group (24.1% vs 10.9%). Exploratory between-group analyses suggested greater improvements in prolonged grief (d = -1.87), post-traumatic stress (d = -1.55), depression (d = -1.03), anxiety (d = -0.71), and self-compassion (d = 1.15) in the immediate intervention group compared with waitlist controls. No statistically significant between-group difference was observed for social disconnection (d = -0.49).
CONCLUSIONS: Therapist-led online bereavement groups appear feasible and acceptable for adults bereaved by cancer and show promise for improving psychological outcomes. A fully powered RCT is warranted to establish efficacy.

Streak break shame vs Resilience.title: Comorbidity of chronic musculoskeletal pain, depression, anxiety and sleep problems.
Streak break shame vs Resilience.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Individuals with chronic pain (CP) are at elevated risk of mental health problems, but the awareness of this issue among patients as well as medical personnel is limited. Chronic musculoskeletal pain (CMP) is the most common type of CP. This narrative review summarizes the latest literature on the comorbidity of CMP with depression, anxiety and sleep problems.
RECENT FINDINGS: Around 40% of CP patients suffer from depression and/or anxiety of clinical severity. Sleep problems affect up to 75% of patients with CP. CMP. Depression, anxiety and impaired sleep are characterized by common underlying physiopathological mechanisms associated with serotonin and noradrenaline neurotransmission, glutamate/γ-aminobutyric acid signaling balance, low Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and altered immune system response. Comorbidity of depression, anxiety and sleep impairment is associated with decline in mental health, functioning and quality of life of the affected individuals, leading to a cumulative disability burden. Evidence supports cognitive behavioral therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy psychotherapies for CMP. Duloxetine is efficacious for pain relief, improvement of mood, anxiety, sleep and quality of life in CMP.
SUMMARY: Comorbidity of psychiatric issues among CMP patients is an unmet need which should be addressed to improve patient outcomes. Mental healthcare specialists ought to be integrated into the teams managing CMP patients.

Digital Mental Health Feasibility.title: A Co-Designed and Bilingual WhatsApp-Based Chatbot Intervention (PflegeBot) for Informal Caregivers in Germany: Single-Arm Nonrandomized Feasibility Study.
Digital Mental Health Feasibility.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Informal caregivers play a central role in long-term care but experience elevated risks of stress, depressive symptoms, and caregiver burden, alongside barriers to accessing preventive support. Low-threshold digital public health interventions may offer scalable support; however, evidence on their feasibility, usability, and contextual fit remains limited, particularly for heterogeneous caregiver populations.
OBJECTIVE: This study describes the development and implementation of PflegeBot, an intersectionality-informed WhatsApp-based chatbot intervention, and evaluates its feasibility, usability, and acceptability among informal caregivers in Germany.
METHODS: A single-arm, nonrandomized feasibility study with pre-post assessments was conducted between December 2023 and March 2024. Informal caregivers aged 18 years and older were recruited via community-based, institutional, and online channels. PflegeBot was a co-designed, bilingual (German and Turkish) WhatsApp-based chatbot that delivered 84 scheduled messages over 12 weeks. Content included caregiving information, self-care, and cognitive behavioral therapy-informed self-help, plus optional frequently asked questions and question functions. Baseline and full follow-up assessments were administered online. Feasibility was assessed using indicators of recruitment, chatbot initiation and message delivery, opt-out, and provision of follow-up measures. Usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS), and acceptability was assessed using study-specific items. Exploratory outcomes included perceived stress (4-item Perceived Stress Scale [PSS-4]), caregiver burden (4-item Zarit Burden Interview [ZBI-4]), depressive symptoms (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale [CES-D]), and loneliness (6-item De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale [DJGLS-6]). Analyses were descriptive; no hypothesis tests were conducted. Open-ended follow-up feedback was examined using a systematic inductive descriptive approach.
RESULTS: Of 102 participants included in the baseline analysis sample, 84 (82%) were women. According to chatbot log data, message delivery was initiated for 67 participants. Forty-nine participants provided at least one follow-up measure, and complete SUS data were available for 46 participants. The mean SUS score was 82.45 (SD 14.86, 95% CI 78.03-86.86; range 47.5-100), and 35 out of 46 (76%) participants scored at or above the benchmark of 68. Overall satisfaction with PflegeBot had a mean rating of 4.02 out of 5 (SD 0.98; n=46). Among participants responding to the relevant item, 1 out of 45 (2%) reported using the optional FAQ function. Mean changes were -0.57 (95% CI -1.24 to 0.10; n=35) for perceived stress, 0.81 (95% CI -0.02 to 1.63; n=36) for caregiver burden, -2.38 (95% CI -5.42 to 0.66; n=34) for depressive symptoms, and -0.39 (95% CI -0.90 to 0.12; n=36) for loneliness. Open-ended feedback highlighted needs for more flexible delivery, greater tailoring, and easier navigation.
CONCLUSIONS: PflegeBot could be delivered through WhatsApp, and participants providing follow-up data reported high usability and generally favorable satisfaction. Controlled evaluations with objective engagement data and assessment of differential reach and outcomes are warranted.

Digital Mental Health Feasibility.title: Feasibility and Preliminary Efficacy of a Digital Cognitive-Behavioral and Expressive Writing Intervention for Fear of Cancer Recurrence in Young Breast Cancer Survivors: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
Digital Mental Health Feasibility.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a 4-week digital intervention combining cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and expressive writing for reducing fear of cancer recurrence (FCR) among young breast cancer survivors (YBCSs).
METHODS: A quasi-experimental, two-group repeated-measures design was employed. The intervention group (n = 14) participated in a 4-week online program with weekly CBT-based group sessions and 20-minute expressive writing sessions on four consecutive days each week (16 sessions in total), whereas the control group (n = 16) received weekly educational materials. Outcomes, including FCR, anxiety, depression, cancer coping, and post-traumatic stress symptoms, were assessed at baseline, immediately postintervention, and 4 weeks postintervention. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA.
RESULTS: Feasibility was supported by a 100% recruitment rate and 100% retention after baseline, with group session attendance (90%), expressive writing completion (95.6%), and weekly telephone consultation completion (80%) all exceeding benchmarks. A significant group × time interaction was observed for FCR (F = 4.888, P = .011), with greater reductions in the intervention group than in the control group over time. Group × time interactions did not reach statistical significance for anxiety, depression, cancer coping, or post-traumatic stress symptoms.
CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrated high feasibility and provided preliminary evidence of a potential benefit of the intervention for reducing FCR among YBCSs. Future randomized controlled trials with larger samples are warranted to confirm these findings and further investigate the mechanisms underlying the intervention effects.
IMPLICATION FOR NURSING PRACTICE: Oncology nurses may consider incorporating accessible, developmentally tailored digital interventions as a potential component of survivorship care for YBCSs.

Digital Mental Health Feasibility.title: Longitudinal Mood Monitoring and Classification of Self-Reported Mental Health Status Using Feels.ai: Feasibility Study.
Digital Mental Health Feasibility.abstract: Purpose This feasibility study evaluated the use of the Feels.ai (Chicago, Illinois) mobile app to collect longitudinal mood data and characterize emotional and behavioral patterns. A secondary objective was to explore whether app-derived behavioral features could distinguish participants with a self-reported mental health condition from those reporting none. Findings were intended to inform future validation studies focused on predictive modeling and clinical applicability. Design This retrospective observational study analyzed de-identified data from 61 college-aged adults who voluntarily enrolled in Feels.ai through social media outreach and recorded mood entries during routine app use. Mental health status was self-reported and was not independently verified through clinical assessment or standardized diagnostic instruments. Methods Participants recorded their mood by selecting from a series of emoji-based facial expressions that were internally mapped to a 0-10 distress scale for quantitative analysis. Numeric scores and descriptive labels were not displayed to participants. App-derived features included mood volatility, mean mood score, mood skewness, skipped days, and the day/night activity ratio. An exploratory random forest classifier was developed to distinguish participants reporting anxiety, depression, or both from those reporting none. Model training used repeated five-fold cross-validation with class upsampling. Missing predictor values were median-imputed within each cross-validation fold. Performance was evaluated using discrimination, classification, and calibration metrics. Logistic regression was evaluated as a conventional comparator using the same resampling and preprocessing approach. Results Across 61 participants, the average adherence rate was 69.7%, with a mean of 15.6 completed days. The random forest achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.74 (95% CI, 0.62-0.86). At a screening-oriented cutoff of 0.30, sensitivity was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.73-0.97), specificity was 0.44 (95% CI, 0.25-0.65), and balanced accuracy was 0.66. The Brier score was 0.21, with a calibration intercept of 0.04 and a calibration slope of 0.59. Logistic regression achieved an AUC of 0.68, which was not significantly different from that of the random forest model (p = 0.27). Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of using Feels.ai for longitudinal mood tracking and deriving behavioral features from routine app use. Exploratory modeling suggests that these features contain signals associated with self-reported mental health status. However, model performance and calibration should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size, self-reported outcomes, missingness in some longitudinal features, and absence of external validation. Larger, more diverse prospective studies using validated clinical measures are needed to determine the reliability, generalizability, and potential clinical utility of these behavioral features.

Digital Mental Health Feasibility.title: Incorporating Objective Behavioral and Biological Measures in a Large-Scale Decentralized Mobile Health Trial for Depression: Randomized Controlled Trial.
Digital Mental Health Feasibility.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Decentralized (ie, fully remote) clinical trials (DCTs) offer a scalable and ecologically valid approach to evaluating digital mental health interventions (DMHIs). Yet, incorporating objective measures of well-being within DCTs poses novel methodological and feasibility challenges that can limit the rigor and precision of data collection in the field.
OBJECTIVE: We recently conducted the Behavior, Biology, and Well-being (BeWell) Study, a large-scale, 3-arm randomized DCT evaluating the Healthy Minds Program app (Humin)-a self-guided DMHI that includes didactic well-being information and meditation components. The current paper's objective is to describe the methodological approach to collecting and processing a multimodal battery of psychological (questionnaires and structured clinical interview), biological (blood and stool assays), and behavioral (stimulus-elicited affect [SEA] task, video log, and Mnemonic Similarity Task [MST]) measures, longitudinally across baseline, the 4-week intervention period, and 17-week follow-up. Secondarily, we evaluate its feasibility.
METHODS: The BeWell Study methodology is described. Descriptive statistics characterized recruitment and retention, as well as data completion and data quality. Binary logistic regressions evaluated whether recruitment sources, demographics, and depression severity predicted measure completion and data quality.
RESULTS: From June 1, 2022, through July 15, 2024, 52,052 individuals started the screening questionnaire. Of these, 2.22% (n=1156 participants; mean age 38.69, SD 12.14 years; women=75.50%; non-Hispanic White=68.88%) completed the screener, met eligibility criteria (including elevated depressive symptoms [Patient Health Questionnaire-9 [PHQ-9] score≥5]), completed baseline measures, were enrolled, and were randomized. Participants were recruited from Craigslist (694/1154, 60.14%), a US-based advertisement website, and university email messages (107/1154, 9.27%); participants were enrolled from every US state. Across the study, 84% (971/1156) of participants were retained (completed ≥1 measure at 17-week follow-up). Across time points, ≥81.40% (941/1156) of participants completed questionnaires and ≥75.17% (869/1156) completed biological samples. Of those completing questionnaires, ≥84.14% (796/946) completed SEA and video log tasks and ≥91.75% (868/946) completed the MST. Of completed assessments, high-quality or analyzable data rates across all time points were ≥97.89% (926/946) for questionnaires, ≥90.20% (773/857) for SEA, ≥84.60% (725/857) for video logs, ≥94.20% (1056/1121) for the MST, ≥98.84% (849/859) for dried blood spots, and ≥99.43% (865/870) for microbiome samples. Greater depressive symptoms at screening, but not age, predicted completion of baseline measures (odds ratios 0.96-0.99; P<.001). For enrolled participants, recruitment sources and baseline depressive symptoms were not predictive of data completion or quality. Older age and having a college degree predicted significantly higher rates of data completion across all data types (questionnaire, behavioral, and biological) at week 4 or week 17 follow-ups.
CONCLUSIONS: This methodological approach offers one model of incorporating objective measures of well-being into DCTs testing DMHIs. Implications and limitations of our approach are discussed.

Digital Mental Health Feasibility.title: Improving weight loss among young adults with excess body weight using a theory-driven digital self-regulation program: a randomized controlled trial.
Digital Mental Health Feasibility.journal: Annals of behavioral medicine : a publication of the Society of Behavioral Medicine
Digital Mental Health Feasibility.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lifestyle modification is fundamental for obesity management but remains challenging.
PURPOSE: To test the effectiveness of a 12-week digital self-regulation program on improving weight loss and self-regulation among young adults.
METHODS: A 2-arm parallel 1:1 randomized controlled trial was conducted. Participants were randomly assigned to either the intervention or the control group. The primary outcomes were weight and self-regulation, while the secondary outcomes were nutrition knowledge, eating phenotypes, overeating habits, anxiety, and depression. All data were collected at weeks 0, 12, and 24.
RESULTS: We showed the effectiveness of a digital commitment device on body weight (-1.90 ± 6.4 kg, P = .002), body mass index (-0.45 ± 2.0 kg/m2, P = .002), waist circumference (-2.10 ± 12.1 cm, P = .01), basal metabolic rate (-20.30 ± 118.6 kcal, P = .04) and body roundness index (-0.17 ± 0.6, P = .014). Interventional effects were sustained for waist circumference (-0.8 ± 2.8 cm, P = .05) and body roundness index (-0.07 ± 0.36, P = .047) 3 months beyond removing access to the commitment device. General improvements in nutrition knowledge, psychological flexibility, uncontrolled eating, and anxiety were found among both groups, but differences were only significant for depression scores (-0.06 ± 1.5, P = .032) and eating self-regulation (0.16 ± 0.54, P = .003).
CONCLUSION: This study showed the potential of a digital commitment device in improving eating self-regulation, anthropometry, and mental wellness for scalable implementation in the community setting.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05969639).
Many young adults struggle with weight management, even when they are motivated to eat healthily. One reason is that everyday stress, food temptations, and busy schedules make it hard to stick to good intentions. This study tested whether a smartphone app designed to strengthen self-regulation skills could help young adults with excess body weight manage their weight more effectively. We conducted a randomized controlled trial in which participants were assigned either to a 12-week digital self-regulation program or to a control group that did not receive the app. The app encouraged users to reflect on their eating habits, manage emotional triggers, and plan ahead for challenging situations, rather than focusing only on calorie counting. Participants who used the app lost more weight by the end of the 12-week program compared with those who did not use it. Interestingly, improvements in eating self-regulation appeared later, 3 months after the program ended, suggesting that these skills may take time to develop. The app also had a low dropout rate, indicating that it was acceptable and easy to use. Overall, this study suggests that digital programs focusing on self-regulation skills may offer a practical and scalable way to support healthy weight management in young adults.

Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.title: Adapting behavioral interventions for traumatic brain injury: strategies to improve treatment receipt and enactment.
Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Behavioral interventions are effective for improving mental and physical health, but individuals with traumatic brain injury (TBI) often experience cognitive and behavioral impairments that limit their ability to engage with and benefit from standard treatments.
PURPOSE: To describe practical adaptations to evidence-based behavioral interventions that enhance treatment receipt (comprehension and engagement) and enactment (application in daily life) for individuals living with TBI.
METHODS: We synthesized adaptation strategies derived from seven clinical trials targeting emotional functioning, problem-solving, and health behaviors in individuals with TBI. Adaptations were organized using a treatment fidelity framework distinguishing treatment receipt and enactment and informed by cognitive rehabilitation principles.
RESULTS: Adaptations to support treatment receipt included simplifying and contextualizing information, increasing repetition, using visual aids, and incorporating structured prompts to accommodate deficits in processing speed, attention, and memory. Process modifications included slower pacing, shorter or more frequent sessions, and integration of remote delivery with technology training and support. Adaptations targeting treatment enactment emphasized habit formation, repeated practice, external memory aids, and technology-based prompts to support prospective memory and initiation. Involvement of care partners and peers further enhanced engagement and generalization of skills.
CONCLUSIONS: Systematic adaptations addressing cognitive and behavioral challenges can improve the accessibility and effectiveness of behavioral interventions for individuals with TBI. Further research should systematically document and evaluate treatment adaptations to determine which modifications are most strongly associated with improved treatment receipt, treatment enactment, implementation outcomes, and clinical benefit across differing cognitive and behavioral profiles.
People living with traumatic brain injury often face challenges such as memory problems, slower thinking, low motivation, and difficulty carrying out plans. These challenges can make it hard to benefit from standard behavioral health programs designed for the general population. At the same time, individuals with traumatic brain injury are at increased risk for mental health challenges, poor physical health, and reduced activity, making effective treatment especially important. This article describes practical ways to adapt proven behavioral treatments so they work better for people with these challenges. Drawing on multiple clinical trials conducted by the authors group and informed by the broader rehabilitation literature, the authors recommend simplifying information, repeating key ideas, and using visual tools to support understanding. Helping individuals practice skills, build routines, and use reminders (such as written notes or phone prompts) may make it easier to apply what they learn in everyday life. Involving a trusted family member or support person can further improve engagement and follow-through. These findings highlight practical strategies to make behavioral treatments more accessible and useful for people living with traumatic brain injury.

Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.title: Multidomain Outcomes of a Digital Self-Management Program in Rural Adults With Chronic Conditions: Single-Arm Prospective Interventional Study.
Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic disease and comorbid mental health problems disproportionately affect rural and underserved populations. Digital self-management programs are potentially scalable, but evaluations often focus on narrow outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: This study examined 12-month longitudinal changes in psychological and multidomain outcomes among Pictou County Patient Empowerment Program participants and explored co-occurring changes and psychological moderators.
METHODS: This single-arm prospective interventional study enrolled 182 community-dwelling adults with ≥1 chronic condition in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, between October 2023 and August 2025 through community-based outreach. Median age was 60 (IQR 51-68) years, 155 of 182 (85.2%) participants were women, and the median number of chronic conditions was 3 (IQR 1-3). The initial 6-month digital intervention delivered brief daily modules targeting physical activity, nutrition, stress regulation, sleep, habit formation, and social connection, followed by a 6-month lower-intensity maintenance period during which monthly group videoconference sessions continued to be offered. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. Primary outcomes were illness perceptions (Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire), perceived stress (10-item Perceived Stress Scale [PSS-10]), disease-related worry (10-item Questionnaire on Distress in Cancer Patients), life satisfaction (Satisfaction With Life Scale), and mental well-being (World Health Organization-Five Well-Being Index [WHO-5]). Secondary outcomes assessed the physical, behavioral, and psychosocial domains. Generalized estimating equations estimated population-averaged longitudinal changes, adjusted for age, sex, relationship status, comorbidity burden, and baseline depression or anxiety medication use. Exploratory models examined co-occurring changes and moderation. Tests were 2-sided with α=.05.
RESULTS: Across outcomes and follow-up assessments, completion ranged from 58.2% (95% CI 51.0%-65.2%; 106/182) to 65.4% (95% CI 58.2%-71.9%; 119/182). At 12 months, illness perceptions decreased (β=-7.3, 95% CI -9.7 to -4.9), perceived stress decreased (β=-2.4, 95% CI -3.5 to -1.3), disease-related worry decreased (β=-6.3, 95% CI -7.8 to -4.7), life satisfaction increased (β=2.5, 95% CI 1.4-3.5), and mental well-being increased (β=10.4, 95% CI 7.2-13.5; all P<.001). Secondary outcomes improved across fatigue, sleep, diet quality, sedentary behavior, spiritual well-being, mental health-related quality of life, weight, and BMI. Exploratory analyses showed that improvements in fatigue, sleep quality, and illness perceptions co-occurred with greater well-being and life satisfaction and lower perceived stress and disease-related worry at both follow-up assessment points. Clinically meaningful stress improvement (≥4-point PSS-10 reduction) was achieved by 36.4% (95% CI 27.3%-45.6%, 39/107) and 43.4% (95% CI 34.0%-52.8%, 46/106) participants at 6 and 12 months, respectively. At 12 months, 43.5% (95% CI 34.2%-52.9%, 47/108) participants reported clinically meaningful improvement in mental well-being (≥10-point WHO-5 increase).
CONCLUSIONS: Participation in this low-bandwidth, home-based digital self-management program was associated with sustained psychological, physical, and behavioral improvements among rural adults with chronic conditions. These multidomain findings support randomized controlled evaluation of scalable digital self-management approaches as adjuncts to rural chronic disease care.

Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.title: Pre-planned reappraisal via implementation intention down-regulates emotional experiences of youth with self-reported depressive symptoms.
Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cognitive reappraisal is an emotion-regulation strategy that involves altering the emotional impact of a situation by changing its appraisal. However, individuals with depressive symptoms often struggle to deploy momentary cognitive reappraisal during emotional encounters due to impaired cognitive control. Pre-planned reappraisal formed through implementation intentions, that is, a strategy rehearsed in advance to activate automatically upon emotional triggers, may offer a more efficient alternative.
AIMS: This study examined whether pre-planned cognitive reappraisal via implementation intentions more effectively reduces negative emotional experience in youth with depressive symptoms than momentary reappraisal, and whether these effects persist after short-term re-exposure.
METHODS: This randomised, single-blind and three-arm experiment was conducted from 10 December 2021 to 19 December 2021 at Southwest University in China. Following screening with the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II), 64 undergraduate students with depressive symptoms (score ≥ 20) and 64 without depressive symptoms (score ≤ 10) were enrolled. Participants were randomly allocated to one of three experimental conditions: passive watching of emotional stimuli, momentary reappraisal (reinterpreting the meaning of a sad face upon presentation) or pre-planned reappraisal (applying a pre-trained reappraisal framework before stimulus presentation). The formal experiment included an emotion elicitation and regulation task, a 20-min interval during which participants completed questionnaires and a re-exposure phase in which all groups passively viewed novel sad faces. Subjective emotional experiences were measured using the nine-point self-assessment manikin (SAM).
RESULTS: Pre-planned reappraisal produced significantly less negative valence and lower arousal ratings for sad faces than passive watching in both participants with and without depressive symptoms. Momentary reappraisal only reduced negative emotional ratings in participants without depressive symptoms, but not those with depressive symptoms. During re-exposure, only prior pre-planned reappraisal yielded sustained reductions in negative emotional ratings. Participants with depressive symptoms also reported greater perceived benefit from pre-planned than from momentary reappraisal.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with momentary reappraisal, pre-planned cognitive reappraisal via implementation intentions produced stronger and more short-term sustained effects among youth with depressive symptoms, supporting its potential use in low-cost self-regulation interventions and clinical cognitive therapies.

Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.title: Habit Learning Shapes Activity Dynamics in the Central Nucleus of the Amygdala.
Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.abstract: Habits develop as motivated behaviors that are strengthened by extended experience and feedback. While the performance component of a habit is relatively well studied, being linked to action-related neural dynamics in the basal ganglia and beyond, neural mechanisms for outcome feedback during habit formation, the reinforcement component, remain unknown. One candidate for this feedback mechanism is in the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA). Here, we identify CeA neural firing dynamics in male and female rats that serve to promote habit formation. We used a novel maze task with rewards of differing identity and value to show that habits arise with task overtraining. After showing that overtraining engages CeA as shown through elevated cFos expression, we recorded in vivo CeA activity across learning and after outcome devaluation when habitual behavior is most identifiable. Neuronal activity changes tracked with habit formation. During learning, a group of recorded cells were significantly responsive at the choice point of maze trials while others encoded outcome consumption. By late training, neural activity exhibited a rapid depression at the choice point of the maze and excitation during reward receipt. In both cases, outcome magnitude, but not identity, was a significant modulator of neural activity. Additionally, a population of neurons tracked instantaneous changes in animal run speed. These speed cells dramatically decreased in number as habits formed. Together, these findings support the role of the CeA in providing reinforcement for habitual behavior, offering a signal that marks successful performance while identifying speed representations in the CeA.

Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.title: Rapid Development and Testing of Behavioral Text Message Reminders for Antidepressant Adherence via Online Panels: Survey Study.
Micro-Habits & Tiny Steps.abstract:
BACKGROUND: SMS text message reminders have been used to promote many health behaviors, such as improving diet and physical activity, managing chronic health conditions, reminding patients about medical appointments, and supporting medication adherence across a range of health conditions. Despite their promise, developing effective reminders tailored to specific patient populations is resource-intensive. AI may facilitate item development, and online research panels may provide an efficient way to test message content with target users prior to implementing large-scale trials.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to (1) develop a library of antidepressant adherence-promoting SMS text messages that are perceived as helpful, (2) test whether an online panel approach can be used to evaluate them, and (3) identify message characteristics perceived as most helpful by patients with depression taking antidepressant medication.
METHODS: In total, 83 SMS text message reminders were developed based on barriers to adherence and behavior change technique pairings, with approximately half authored by the study team, and half generated by AI. Using an online panel, we recruited 181 American adults with depression currently prescribed an antidepressant medication. Each participant rated a subset of messages on how much they thought each would help them remember to take their medication. Associations between message characteristics and ratings were estimated using generalized linear models in Stata. Survey weights were used in analyses to align the sample with national antidepressant user demographics.
RESULTS: The online panel was able to rapidly recruit a sample of participants, who provided 7520 item ratings in total. AI-generated messages were rated as significantly more helpful than those authored by humans (adjusted mean difference 0.24 on a 5-point scale, 95% CI 0.12-0.36; P<.001). Messages addressing delayed symptom benefit were preferred over other adherence barriers, and behavior change techniques emphasizing self-monitoring (P<.001), habit formation (P<.001), and natural consequences (P<.001) received significantly higher ratings than those using external influence or support. No difference was observed between motivational and informational message content.
CONCLUSIONS: Online panels offer a rapid, scalable approach to evaluating SMS text message reminders for patients currently taking antidepressants. When provided with specific instructions and human-led examples, AI can efficiently generate message content perceived to be helpful in promoting medication adherence. Given that AI-generated content received higher ratings than human-authored messages, future work may consider using this tool to support rapid intervention development. In addition, identifying common barriers to adherence and applying behavior change techniques to address those barriers can inform targeted message development and support adherence. Taken together, these findings demonstrate the utility of combining low-cost methods such as online panel research with AI to accelerate the design and preliminary evaluation of digital health interventions.
